name: Subadditivity effect
statement: Fifty UK intelligence analysts, split between two conditions, gave four exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses probabilities summing to 1.54 and 1.77, where probability theory requires one.
meaning: Probability theory is extensional. Two descriptions of the same event must carry the same probability, and the probability of an event must equal the sum of the probabilities of its disjoint parts. Judged probability does neither. Tversky and Koehler's support theory attaches probability to descriptions rather than to events, calls those descriptions hypotheses, and gives each one a support value standing for the strength of evidence behind it. The judged probability of a focal hypothesis is its support divided by the combined support of the focal and the alternative hypothesis. Support is assumed to grow as a description is broken into parts, so the support of "homicide" is at most that of "homicide by an acquaintance or homicide by a stranger", which is at most the sum of the support of the two components. Two consequences follow and are routinely confused. Implicit subadditivity is a single judgment of a detailed description coming out above the judgment of the packed description. Explicit subadditivity is components judged separately summing above the disjunction judged whole. The same equations predict that two complementary hypotheses sum to one, so this is a claim about partitions of three or more, not about probability judgment in general.

origin.who: Amos Tversky and Derek J. Koehler
origin.note: "Support theory: A nonextensional representation of subjective probability" set out the support function and the unpacking prediction, and gave the effect its formal treatment rather than its first sighting. Its first study put causes of death to 120 Stanford undergraduates. One group gave the implicit category "unnatural cause" a mean of 32%, while a separate group's estimates of accident, homicide and other unnatural cause summed to 53%. That 53% is a sum of three judgments made by different people, not one judgment of a longer description, so the comparison shows explicit subadditivity. The pattern predates the theory by sixteen years. Bearden, Wallsten and Fox describe Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein's 1978 fault-tree study, in which car mechanics put the chance that a car fails to start for reasons other than the battery, fuel system or engine at 22 in 100, while a second group given that residual broken into starting system, ignition system, mischief and a smaller residual returned judgments summing to 44 in 100. The 1977 Decision Research technical report behind that article prints the two means as 0.215 and 0.441.

evidence: Koehler, Brenner and Tversky asked 115 Stanford students and staff to judge, for a student known to major in a social science, the probability of each of four majors, one major at a time. Totals came to 2.18 given a statistics course, 1.96 given Western Civilization, 1.61 given French literature and 1.42 given modern physics. Seven of the 115 had totals at or below one. The contrast between the two typical courses and the two atypical ones gave t(1701) = 9.43, p < 0.001, the enhancement effect: evidence compatible with every hypothesis raises the total. A second experiment on 170 undergraduates gave probability totals of 1.87 and 1.57 for the two courses and frequency totals of 1.61 and 1.11, so frequency wording lowered the totals without removing them. In two crime stories the totals rose from 1.67 to 1.94 and from 1.43 to 1.81 as more evidence was disclosed. Fox and Birke put the same tests to practising attorneys. Each lawyer was assigned at random to judge one event, and the totals below are sums of the median judgment of each separate group. Two hundred lawyers at a national American Bar Association meeting in November 1997, median 17 years in practice, judged how Jones v. Clinton would end. The two-way split summed to 0.95, which did not differ from one, and the five-way split to 1.49, t(115) = 6.49, p < 0.0001. Oregon attorneys recruited at a continuing legal education programme, 31 of them, and at a state bar conference, 24 more, priced a tort claim. Their medians for four award ranges summed to 1.78, t(46) = 4.28, p < 0.0001. A separate group of 138 lawyers, 41 at an American Bar Association session on tort and insurance practice and 97 at a Californian continuing legal education programme, was asked whether to advise accepting a settlement. Of the 66 told the problems of proof concerned "liability", 52% said accept; of the 72 told they concerned "duty, breach, or causation", 74% did, with a chi-square of 7.22 on one degree of freedom, p < 0.01. Fox, Rogers and Tversky took the question to trading floors. Their study of decision under uncertainty drew 32 people at the Pacific Stock Exchange, 15 options traders and 17 support staff, with median floor experience of five years, and 28 at the Chicago Board Options Exchange, 19 traders and 9 support staff, with nearly four years. Judging events defined by a stock's closing price two weeks ahead, 55 of the 60 points fell below the identity line on both tests, p < 0.001 by sign test. The mean sum of judged probabilities of two disjoint events was 0.84 against 0.68 for their union, a gap of 0.16, or about 24%. Minimum selling prices for the matching prospects gave decision weights of 0.84 against 0.65, a gap of 0.19, or about 29%. Both percentages are the paper's own rather than this entry's arithmetic. Five of the Pacific subjects were dropped for not following the pricing instructions, so the decision weights rest on 55 of the 60. A footnote records that the median sums for an event and its complement were 1.00, 0.96, 1.00 and 0.99 for the four stocks.

examples.tag: The causes of a slipped launch
examples.text: Asked one at a time, a team puts the chance the launch slips for engineering reasons at forty percent, for supply reasons at thirty-five, and for approvals at thirty. Asked instead for the chance it slips at all, the same team says sixty.

examples.tag: The holiday budget broken into lines
examples.text: Travel, rooms, food and outings, each estimated on its own, add to more than the figure the same person gives for the trip as a whole. Splitting a description into named parts raises the support behind it.

examples.tag: The question with only two answers
examples.text: Asked whether a bid will be won or lost, a manager gives two figures that come to about one. The excess needs a partition of three or more branches, so this is not a claim that judged probabilities always overshoot.

replication.headline: The pattern reproduces in students, physicians, options traders, lawyers and serving intelligence analysts, and a structured technique built to force consideration of alternatives left it in place.
replication.detail: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami gave 50 UK intelligence analysts a case with four mutually exclusive and exhaustive hypotheses. The four probabilities summed to 1.54 in the control condition, bootstrapped 95% CI 1.33 to 1.76, and to 1.77 among analysts trained in and using the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, 95% CI 1.56 to 1.97, both p < 0.001, with 25 analysts in each. Summed across the two implicit disjunctions, analysts gave them 0.56 less probability than their constituents took in the control condition and 0.82 less in the trained one, p < 0.001 in both. Those are condition totals, not one figure for each disjunction. Training in the technique did not help. The unpacking effect ran larger in the trained condition by 0.22, which did not reach significance at p = 0.13, and mean additivity violation was also greater there, by 0.25, t(48) = 1.81, p = 0.08. These were trainees rather than veterans, with mean age 27.79 years and mean experience as an analyst of 14.08 months. Binary complements behaved as support theory predicts, summing to 0.98 in the control condition and 0.95 in the other. Karvetski and Mandel repeated the comparison on 227 participants recruited through Qualtrics Panels and again found the technique gave no advantage across their tests of coherence, with subadditivity present in both groups. That study used two hypotheses rather than four, and it found their probabilities subadditive in all six cases, which the authors say contradicts support theory's binary complementarity axiom. Mean bias from complementarity rose with the total evidential support in the case, from 0.13 at the low level to 0.18 at the medium and 0.21 at the high, and correlated with support at r(225) = 0.29. Only the step up from the low level was significant; medium against high reached p = 0.06. All six cases carried total evidential support above one, which the authors give as the reason they saw subadditivity alone where earlier work saw both directions. The 2018 paper reports that two earlier experiments by Mandel on undergraduates produced a mean unpacking factor of 2.4, the ratio of the summed unpacked estimates to the packed estimate, for forecasts of terrorism split into acts by Al Qaeda and acts by operatives unaffiliated with it. That figure is quoted here from the 2018 paper's description rather than read from Mandel's 2005 article.

study.cite: Mandel, D. R., Karvetski, C. W., & Dhami, M. K. (2018). Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? Judgment and Decision Making, 13(6), 607-621.

limits: The direction of the effect reverses under two known conditions. The first is atypicality. Bearden, Wallsten and Fox report that Sloman and colleagues found a median judged probability of 0.55 that a randomly selected death is due to "disease", 0.60 for "heart disease, cancer, stroke, or any other disease", and 0.40 for "pneumonia, diabetes, cirrhosis, or any other disease". Those medians are quoted from that description rather than read from the 2004 paper. The citation carrying them names Stibel as a co-author, where the same paper's own reference list and Crossref both name Wisniewski. The second is fluency. Redden and Frederick showed 151 undergraduates three versions of one die gamble, its winning event described as "getting an even number", "getting a 2, 4, or 6" or "getting a 1, 4, or 6". The packed version was rated more likely, 4.2 against a pooled 3.9 on a seven-point scale, t(150) = 4.02, p < 0.01, and more attractive against a sure $15, 5.4 against a pooled 4.9 on an eleven-point scale, t(150) = 2.84, p < 0.01. They argue that added detail costs processing fluency and that dysfluency reads as low likelihood, opposing the usual effect. A third limit is that part of the phenomenon may be arithmetic. Bearden, Wallsten and Fox show formally that random error in mapping a private judgment onto a bounded response scale is enough to make mean judgments subadditive even when the private judgments are additive, and their first study, on 41 participants trained with feedback to say which of two invisible targets a ball on a screen was aimed at, found unpacking ratios of 1.15 on means and 1.14 on medians. They stress that the subadditivity there was small. Those two figures are read from the authors' manuscript hosted at UCLA rather than from the published version in the Journal of Mathematical Psychology. Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, PubMed and the Open Science Framework, including its registrations, found no meta-analysis of the effect and no multi-laboratory replication of it. OpenAlex answered every query that day with a server error, so its leg of an earlier search could not be repeated. The nearest preregistered work found is Ding and Feldman's Registered Report on partition dependence, a neighbouring effect in which the framing of a question sets the default split of the outcome space, which reran Fox and Rottenstreich on 603 Prolific participants and reported a mostly successful replication, three of its four target studies holding and the fourth not. Tversky and Koehler's 1994 paper and Rottenstreich and Tversky's 1997 paper were read in full in the authorised reprints in Tversky's Selected Writings, published by MIT Press in 2004. Three sources stayed shut on 21 September 2026: Sloman and colleagues 2004, Mandel 2005, and the full text of Redelmeier, Koehler, Liberman and Tversky, whose abstract was read at PubMed. So did the Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein article of record, though the 1977 technical report behind it was read in full.
misreadings: The commonest error is reading this as the conjunction fallacy under another name. The conjunction fallacy compares an event with a subset of itself, bank teller against feminist bank teller, and the mistake is rating the subset higher. Subadditivity compares an event with its own parts added up, and the mistake is rating the whole lower than the sum. The two run in opposite directions across the same axiom, and entry 75 covers the first. The second error is that judged probabilities always add to more than one. Complementary pairs usually come out at about one: 0.98 and 0.95 among the intelligence analysts, 0.95 among the lawyers judging Jones v. Clinton, and medians of 1.00, 0.96, 1.00 and 0.99 across the four stocks the options traders priced. The excess normally needs a partition of three or more. Karvetski and Mandel are the exception located here, reporting subadditive complementary pairs in all six of their cases and stating that this contradicts the axiom. Third, unpacking is described as always raising judged probability. It raises it when the parts named are typical and easy to read, and lowers it when they are atypical or hard to read. Fourth, expertise is treated as a defence. Options traders with four and five years on the floor, attorneys with a median of 17 years in practice, and serving intelligence analysts all showed the effect, and the technique the intelligence community recommends for weighing competing hypotheses did not remove it. The analysts are the weakest of those three cases, since their mean experience in the role was 14.08 months, so the lawyers and the traders carry the point. Fifth, the mechanism is often given as memory alone, on the view that naming the parts reminds a judge of possibilities that were overlooked. Bearden, Wallsten and Fox argue this cannot be the whole account, because subadditivity also turns up when one numerical dimension such as a stock price is cut into intervals, where no forgotten possibility is being recovered, and because random response error alone reproduces the pattern.

sources.text: Tversky, A., & Koehler, D. J. (1994). Support theory: A nonextensional representation of subjective probability. Psychological Review, 101(4), 547-567. Metadata verified at Crossref. The article itself is closed at the publisher, but it is reprinted in full, with the publisher's permission, as chapter 14 of Amos Tversky's Selected Writings, edited by Eldar Shafir for MIT Press in 2004, and that text was read at https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~gary/PAPER-SUGGESTIONS/Preference,%20Belief,%20and%20Similarity%20Selected%20Writings%20(Bradford%20Books).pdf. The theory statement, the causes of death study and its unpacking factor of 1.66 are read there. A scanned copy of the article is also deposited at https://zenodo.org/records/1066966.

Koehler, D. J., Brenner, L. A., & Tversky, A. (1997). The enhancement effect in probability judgment. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 10(4), 293-313. Read in the copy hosted at https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/papers/koehler-brenner-tversky-jbdm1997.pdf.

Fox, C. R., & Birke, R. (2002). Forecasting trial outcomes: Lawyers assign higher probability to possibilities that are described in greater detail. Law and Human Behavior, 26(2), 159-173. Read in the copy hosted at http://personal.anderson.ucla.edu/policy.area/faculty/fox/lhb02.pdf.

Fox, C. R., Rogers, B. A., & Tversky, A. (1996). Options traders exhibit subadditive decision weights. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 13(1), 5-17. Read as a scanned copy hosted at http://personal.anderson.ucla.edu/policy.area/faculty/fox/jru96.pdf, which carries no text layer, so all thirteen pages were put through optical character recognition and the figures searched in the result.

Mandel, D. R., Karvetski, C. W., & Dhami, M. K. (2018). Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? Judgment and Decision Making, 13(6), 607-621. Read in the copy hosted at https://journal.sjdm.org/18/18803/jdm18803.pdf.

Karvetski, C. W., & Mandel, D. R. (2020). Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help? Judgment and Decision Making, 15(6), 939-958. Read in the copy hosted at https://journal.sjdm.org/20/200430/jdm200430.pdf.

Redden, J. P., & Frederick, S. (2011). Unpacking unpacking: Greater detail can reduce perceived likelihood. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 140(2), 159-167. Read in the copy hosted at https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/unpacking_unpacking.pdf.

Bearden, J. N., Wallsten, T. S., & Fox, C. R. (2007). Contrasting stochastic and support theory accounts of subadditivity. Journal of Mathematical Psychology, 51(4), 229-241. Figures here are read from the authors' manuscript version, "A stochastic model of subadditivity", hosted at http://personal.anderson.ucla.edu/policy.area/faculty/fox/bearden_wallsten_fox_10-04.pdf, not from the published article, which stayed shut on 21 September 2026. The two versions carry different titles and have not been compared.

Sloman, S., Rottenstreich, Y., Wisniewski, E., Hadjichristidis, C., & Fox, C. R. (2004). Typical versus atypical unpacking and superadditive probability judgment. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 30(3), 573-582. Author list and metadata verified at Crossref. Still shut on 21 September 2026 after the publisher, Semantic Scholar, the author pages and the Wayback Machine were tried. The one open copy any index names, in the University of Trento repository, is served only behind that university's single sign-on, which is a login wall and not a paywall. The medians quoted here therefore come from Bearden, Wallsten and Fox's description. That description's in-text citation names Stibel as a co-author, where its own reference list and Crossref both name Wisniewski.

Rottenstreich, Y., & Tversky, A. (1997). Unpacking, repacking, and anchoring: Advances in support theory. Psychological Review, 104(2), 406-415. Metadata verified at Crossref. Read in full in the authorised reprint as chapter 16 of Tversky's Selected Writings, MIT Press, 2004. Its homicide study gave median judgments of 0.20 for homicide against accidental death, 0.25 for the explicit disjunction of homicide by an acquaintance or by a stranger, and 0.15 for each component separately.

Brenner, L., & Rottenstreich, Y. (1999). Focus, repacking, and the judgment of grouped hypotheses. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 12(2), 141-148. Read in the copy hosted at https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/papers/brenner-rottenstreich-jbdm1999.pdf.

Redelmeier, D. A., Koehler, D. J., Liberman, V., & Tversky, A. (1995). Probability judgment in medicine: Discounting unspecified possibilities. Medical Decision Making, 15(3), 227-230. Abstract read at PubMed. The full text stayed shut on 21 September 2026, the publisher answering a Cloudflare challenge rather than a payment page. Tversky and Koehler describe the study: 59 Stanford physicians judged an abdominal pain case, and the residual category took a mean of 0.50 where two diagnoses were named against 0.69 for its unpacked components where five were, p < 0.005 by Mann-Whitney test. Those figures are read from Tversky and Koehler's account of the study while it was still unpublished, not from the article. The title travels in three forms: Crossref records it without a subtitle, PubMed spells the second word "judgement", and Koehler, Brenner and Tversky's reference list ends it "discounting unspecified causes".

Mandel, D. R. (2005). Are risk assessments of a terrorist attack coherent? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 11(4), 277-288. Metadata verified at Crossref. Still shut on 21 September 2026 after the publisher, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, the Open Science Framework and the author's institution were tried; the two CiteSeerX records OpenAlex lists could not be reached from this session at all, and the Defence Technical Information Center was serving a maintenance page. The unpacking factor of 2.4 is quoted from Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018).

Fischhoff, B., Slovic, P., & Lichtenstein, S. (1978). Fault trees: Sensitivity of estimated failure probabilities to problem representation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 4(2), 330-344. Metadata verified at Crossref; the article of record was not opened. The technical report it grew from, "Fault trees: Sensitivity of estimated failure probabilities to problem representation", Decision Research PTR-1042-77-8, August 1977, was opened and searched at https://bitsavers.trailing-edge.com/pdf/perceptronics/Decision_Research/ADA057163_Fischhoff_-_Fault_Trees_-_Sensitivity_of_Estimated_Failure_Probabilities_to_Problem_Representation_197708.pdf. Its experiment six gives the two means as 0.215 and 0.441, which Bearden, Wallsten and Fox round to 22 and 44 in 100. Whether the published article prints the same numbers has not been checked.

Ding, K., & Feldman, G. (2025). Revisiting partition priming in judgement under uncertainty: replication and extension Registered Report of Fox and Rottenstreich (2003). Royal Society Open Science, 12(7). Read in the PubMed Central copy.
